------------------------------------------------------------------------
STUDY — English Meter
Beat and offbeat: iambic pentameter, the trochaic line, and the ballad stanza
------------------------------------------------------------------------

@deck enmeter
Title: English Meter
Small heading: Beat and offbeat: iambic pentameter, the trochaic line, and the ballad stanza
Sources: The ordinary English grammar, and Reed and Kellogg’s diagram

@panel 1

**STRESS AND THE FOOT.** English meter counts stressed syllables and arranges the unstressed ones between them. A **foot** is one stressed syllable with its unstressed ones: the **iamb** (unstressed, stressed: “a-WAY”), the **trochee** (“TI-ger”), the **anapest** (“in-ter-VENE”), and the **dactyl** (“MUR-mur-ing”).

The stress of a word does not move for the meter: a line fits its meter when the beats fall on syllables the words already stress, or on syllables that can take a light stress.

Question: What does English meter count?

Choices:
- Stressed syllables, with the unstressed ones arranged between them.
- Long and short syllables, as Latin does.
- The letters in each line.
- Only the rhymes.

Answer: Stressed syllables, with the unstressed ones arranged between them.

Why: English verse is accentual-syllabic: it counts beats and, in most meters, syllables too.


@panel 2

**IAMBIC PENTAMETER.** Five iambs: ten syllables, with the stress on the even ones. “Shall I com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer’s DAY” is heard as “shall I | com-PARE | thee TO | a SUM | mer’s DAY,” with a light beat on “to.”

Unrhymed, it is **blank verse**, the line of Shakespeare’s plays, of *Paradise Lost*, and of Tennyson’s “Ulysses.” Rhymed in pairs, it is the **heroic couplet** of Pope. In fourteen lines with a set rhyme scheme it makes the **sonnet**.

Question: How many syllables has a regular line of iambic pentameter?

Choices:
- Ten
- Eight
- Twelve
- Five

Answer: Ten

Why: Five feet of two syllables each.


@panel 3

**VARIATION.** Few lines are perfectly regular. The commonest change is a trochee in the first foot: “DEATH, be | not PROUD.” A line may also end with an extra unstressed syllable, a **feminine ending**. The meter is the pattern the ear expects, and the variations are heard against it.

Question: “DEATH, be not PROUD” begins with…

Choices:
- A trochee in place of the first iamb
- An anapest
- A spondee in every foot
- A feminine ending

Answer: A trochee in place of the first iamb

Why: The first foot is reversed, stressed then unstressed; the line returns to iambs.


@panel 4

**THE TROCHAIC LINE.** Trochaic lines begin on the beat. English trochaic tetrameter usually drops its last unstressed syllable, so that the line also ends on a beat: “TY-ger | TY-ger | BURN-ing | BRIGHT” has seven syllables and four beats.

Question: Why has “Tyger Tyger, burning bright” only seven syllables?

Choices:
- The last trochee has lost its unstressed syllable
- One word is not counted
- It is iambic pentameter
- The meter counts only nouns

Answer: The last trochee has lost its unstressed syllable

Why: Four trochees would have eight syllables; the last is cut to a single beat.


@panel 5

**THE BALLAD STANZA.** Four lines, of four beats and three beats in turn, usually rhyming the second and fourth: “It is an ancient Mariner, / And he stoppeth one of three.” When the lines are strictly iambic, eight syllables and six, hymn books call it **common meter**. The ballad lets an extra unstressed syllable in where it likes.

Question: The lines of the ballad stanza have…

Choices:
- Four beats and three beats in turn
- Five beats each
- Six beats and five in turn
- Two beats each

Answer: Four beats and three beats in turn

Why: 4, 3, 4, 3, with the rhyme usually on the three-beat lines.


@panel 6

**HOW TO SCAN.** Read the line naturally and mark the syllables that the words themselves stress. Then find the pattern that fits most of the line, count the beats, and name the meter by its foot and the number of feet: iambic pentameter, trochaic tetrameter. Last, note where the line varies, and whether it rhymes.

Question: The first step in scanning an English line is…

Choices:
- To mark the syllables the words themselves stress
- To count the letters
- To find the rhyme
- To decide the meter before reading

Answer: To mark the syllables the words themselves stress

Why: The meter is found from the stresses of the words, not imposed on them.


------------------------------------------------------------------------
STUDY — English Poetry
Ten passages of English verse, read part by part
------------------------------------------------------------------------

@deck enpoetry
Title: English Poetry
Small heading: Ten passages of English verse, read part by part
Sources: The ordinary English grammar, and Reed and Kellogg’s diagram

@panel 1

**Milton, *Paradise Lost* I.1–6 · Blank verse**

Of Man’s first disobedience, and the fruit
Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste
Brought death into the World, and all our woe,
With loss of Eden, till one greater Man
Restore us, and regain the blissful seat,
Sing, Heavenly Muse,

**Context.** John Milton’s epic, published in 1667, opens as the classical epics do, by naming its subject and calling on the Muse. The main verb, “Sing,” is held back to the sixth line. The meter is blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter.


@panel 2

**The subject of the song, placed first.** “Of Man’s first disobedience, and the fruit”: “Of” begins the phrase that names what the Muse is to sing of; its two objects are “disobedience” and “the fruit.”


@panel 3

**A relative clause.** “Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste”: “Whose mortal taste” begins a relative clause describing the tree: whose deadly taste brought death.


@panel 4

**The verb of the relative clause.** “Brought death into the World, and all our woe”: “Brought” has two objects, “death” and “all our woe,” and the second is held to the end of the line.


@panel 5

**A clause of time.** “till one greater Man”: “Till” begins a clause of time whose verbs, “restore” and “regain,” come in the next line, in the subjunctive of an event awaited.


@panel 6

**The main verb.** “Sing, Heavenly Muse,”: “Sing” is an imperative, and “Heavenly Muse” is the noun of address. Five lines of phrases and clauses come before it.


@panel 7

“Of Man’s first disobedience”

Question: What does the phrase beginning “Of Man’s first disobedience” complete?

Choices:
- The verb “Sing,” five lines later
- The verb “Brought”
- The noun “tree”
- The verb “Restore”

Answer: The verb “Sing,” five lines later

Why: The Muse is asked to sing of these things; the verb is held to the sixth line.


@panel 8

“whose mortal taste”

Question: “Whose mortal taste brought death” is…

Choices:
- A relative clause describing “tree”
- The main clause
- A clause of time
- A noun clause

Answer: A relative clause describing “tree”

Why: “Whose” takes up the tree.


@panel 9

“Restore”

Question: Why is it “restore” and not “restores”?

Choices:
- It is the subjunctive after “till,” of an event still awaited
- It is an imperative
- The subject is plural
- It is an infinitive

Answer: It is the subjunctive after “till,” of an event still awaited

Why: “Till one greater Man restore us” looks forward to an event, and older English uses the subjunctive.


@panel 10

“Sing”

Question: “Sing” is…

Choices:
- An imperative, the main verb of the period
- A present indicative
- An infinitive
- A participle

Answer: An imperative, the main verb of the period

Why: It is a command to the Muse, the noun of address that follows.


@panel 11

**Shakespeare, *Sonnets* 18.1–8 · Iambic pentameter**

Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d,
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance, or nature’s changing course untrimm’d:

**Context.** Shakespeare’s sonnets were printed in 1609. A sonnet has fourteen lines of iambic pentameter; these are the first eight, which set the beloved against a summer’s day.


@panel 12

**A question.** “Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?”: The poem opens with a question, with the helping verb “shall” before the subject. “Thee” is the older objective form of “you.”


@panel 13

**Comparatives.** “Thou art more lovely and more temperate”: “Thou art” is the older second person singular of “be,” and the comparatives “more lovely” and “more temperate” complete it.


@panel 14

**The emphatic “do”.** “Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May”: “Do shake” is the present with “do,” which here fills out the meter and adds emphasis.


@panel 15

**Inversion.** “Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines”: The adjective “too hot” stands first, before the subject “the eye of heaven” and the verb “shines.”


@panel 16

**A passive with inversion.** “And often is his gold complexion dimm’d”: The helping verb “is” comes before the subject, “his gold complexion,” and “dimm’d” completes the passive.


@panel 17

“thee”

Question: “Thee” is…

Choices:
- The older objective form of the second person singular
- The subject
- A possessive
- A plural

Answer: The older objective form of the second person singular

Why: “Thou” is the subject form, and “thee” the object.


@panel 18

“more lovely and more temperate”

Question: “More lovely and more temperate” are…

Choices:
- Comparative adjectives completing “art”
- Adverbs modifying “compare”
- Superlatives
- Nouns

Answer: Comparative adjectives completing “art”

Why: They follow the linking verb and describe “thou.”


@panel 19

“do shake”

Question: In “Rough winds do shake,” what is “do”?

Choices:
- A helping verb of emphasis in the present
- The main verb meaning “perform”
- A sign of the future
- A sign of the passive

Answer: A helping verb of emphasis in the present

Why: “Do” with the plain verb makes an emphatic present.


@panel 20

“is his gold complexion dimm’d”

Question: “Is his gold complexion dimm’d” is…

Choices:
- A passive verb, with the subject after the helping verb
- A question
- An active verb
- A participle alone

Answer: A passive verb, with the subject after the helping verb

Why: The order is inverted: his gold complexion is dimmed.


@panel 21

**Gray, *Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard* stanza 1 · Iambic pentameter, in quatrains**

The curfew tolls the knell of parting day;
The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea;
The plowman homeward plods his weary way,
And leaves the world to darkness and to me.

**Context.** Thomas Gray published his Elegy in 1751. Each stanza has four lines of iambic pentameter rhyming alternately. The first stanza sets the scene at nightfall.


@panel 22

**Subject, verb, object.** “The curfew tolls the knell of parting day”: “The curfew” is the subject, “tolls” the verb, and “the knell” the object; “parting” is a participle describing “day.”


@panel 23

**A collective noun.** “The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea”: “Herd” is a collective noun, and Gray gives it a plural verb, “wind,” thinking of the many cattle.


@panel 24

**An adverb placed early.** “The plowman homeward plods his weary way”: “Homeward” stands before the verb “plods,” and “his weary way” is its object.


@panel 25

**A second verb.** “And leaves the world to darkness and to me”: “And” joins a second verb, “leaves,” to “plods,” with the same subject.


@panel 26

“parting”

Question: “Parting” in “parting day” is…

Choices:
- A participle used as an adjective
- A gerund
- A verb in the past
- A noun

Answer: A participle used as an adjective

Why: It describes “day”: the departing day.


@panel 27

“wind”

Question: Why is “wind” plural with “herd”?

Choices:
- “Herd” is a collective noun, here taken as many animals
- It is an error
- “Wind” is a noun
- The verb agrees with “lea”

Answer: “Herd” is a collective noun, here taken as many animals

Why: A collective noun may take a plural verb when its members are thought of one by one.


@panel 28

“homeward”

Question: “Homeward” is…

Choices:
- An adverb of direction modifying “plods”
- An adjective describing “plowman”
- A noun
- A preposition

Answer: An adverb of direction modifying “plods”

Why: It tells where he plods.


@panel 29

“leaves”

Question: What is the subject of “leaves”?

Choices:
- “The plowman”
- “The herd”
- “The world”
- “Darkness”

Answer: “The plowman”

Why: “And” joins “leaves” to “plods,” and both have the subject “the plowman.”


@panel 30

**Coleridge, *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner* lines 1–8 · The ballad stanza**

It is an ancient Mariner,
And he stoppeth one of three.
"By thy long grey beard and glittering eye,
Now wherefore stopp'st thou me?

"The Bridegroom's doors are opened wide,
And I am next of kin;
The guests are met, the feast is set:
May'st hear the merry din."

**Context.** Coleridge’s poem appeared in Lyrical Ballads in 1798. It is written in the ballad stanza: lines of four and three beats in turn. An old sailor stops a guest on his way to a wedding.


@panel 31

**An introducing “it”.** “It is an ancient Mariner”: “It is” introduces the person spoken of, as in older ballads.


@panel 32

**The older ending “-eth”.** “And he stoppeth one of three”: “Stoppeth” is the older form of “stops,” the third person singular.


@panel 33

**A question.** “Now wherefore stopp'st thou me?”: “Wherefore” means “why,” and “stopp’st thou” is the older second person singular with the subject after the verb.


@panel 34

**Two clauses side by side.** “The guests are met, the feast is set”: Two short clauses stand without a conjunction; “are met” and “is set” describe a state.


@panel 35

“stoppeth”

Question: “Stoppeth” is…

Choices:
- The older third person singular, “stops”
- A past tense
- A plural
- An imperative

Answer: The older third person singular, “stops”

Why: The ending “-eth” is the older form of “-s.”


@panel 36

“wherefore”

Question: “Wherefore” means…

Choices:
- “Why”
- “Where”
- “Therefore”
- “Whereas”

Answer: “Why”

Why: In older English “wherefore” asks for the reason.


@panel 37

“thou”

Question: In “stopp’st thou me,” the subject is…

Choices:
- “Thou,” placed after the verb in a question
- “Me”
- “Beard”
- “Eye”

Answer: “Thou,” placed after the verb in a question

Why: The question puts the verb before its subject, and “me” is the object.


@panel 38

“May'st hear”

Question: In “May’st hear the merry din,” what is left out?

Choices:
- The subject “thou”
- The verb
- The object
- Nothing

Answer: The subject “thou”

Why: “Mayst” is the second person singular, and its subject is understood.


@panel 39

**Wordsworth, *“I wandered lonely as a Cloud”* stanza 1, text of 1807 · Iambic tetrameter**

I wandered lonely as a Cloud
That floats on high o'er Vales and Hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd
A host of dancing Daffodills;
Along the Lake, beneath the trees,
Ten thousand dancing in the breeze.

**Context.** William Wordsworth published this poem in 1807. The lines are iambic tetrameter, four iambs each. The first stanza is one sentence.


@panel 40

**The main clause and a comparison.** “I wandered lonely as a Cloud”: “I wandered” is the main clause, “lonely” describes “I,” and “as a Cloud” makes a comparison.


@panel 41

**A relative clause.** “That floats on high o'er Vales and Hills”: “That” takes up “a Cloud.”


@panel 42

**A clause of time.** “When all at once I saw a crowd”: “When” begins a dependent clause, and “a crowd” is the object of “saw.”


@panel 43

**An appositive.** “A host of dancing Daffodills”: “A host” renames “a crowd,” and “dancing” is a participle describing the daffodils.


@panel 44

**A phrase without a verb.** “Ten thousand dancing in the breeze”: “Ten thousand dancing” is another appositive phrase; it has a participle but no finite verb.


@panel 45

“lonely”

Question: “Lonely” in “I wandered lonely” describes…

Choices:
- “I,” the subject
- “Wandered,” as an adverb
- “Cloud”
- “Hills”

Answer: “I,” the subject

Why: “Lonely” is an adjective, so it describes the one who wandered.


@panel 46

“That floats”

Question: “That floats on high” is…

Choices:
- A relative clause describing “a Cloud”
- A noun clause
- A clause of time
- The main clause

Answer: A relative clause describing “a Cloud”

Why: “That” takes up the cloud.


@panel 47

“When all at once”

Question: “When all at once I saw a crowd” is…

Choices:
- A dependent clause of time
- The main clause
- A relative clause
- An indirect question

Answer: A dependent clause of time

Why: “When” subordinates it to “I wandered.”


@panel 48

“A host”

Question: “A host of dancing Daffodills” stands…

Choices:
- In apposition to “a crowd”
- As the subject of “saw”
- As a second main clause
- As a noun of address

Answer: In apposition to “a crowd”

Why: It renames the crowd that he saw.


@panel 49

**Shelley, *Ozymandias* lines 1–8 · Iambic pentameter, a sonnet (in the drill)**

I met a traveller from an antique land
Who said: Two vast and trunkless legs of stone
Stand in the desert … Near them, on the sand,
Half sunk, a shattered visage lies, whose frown,
And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command,
Tell that its sculptor well those passions read
Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things,
The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed:

**Context.** Shelley’s sonnet of 1818. The traveler’s report runs on past the line ends, and its second sentence has a long subject and a verb, “Tell,” held to the sixth line.


@panel 50

**The frame.** “I met a traveller from an antique land
Who said”: “Who said” is a relative clause on “a traveller.” All that follows is what he said. The line scans as five iambs: “i MET a TRAV-el-LER from AN an-TIQUE LAND,” with a light stress on “-ler.”


@panel 51

**The report begins.** “Two vast and trunkless legs of stone
Stand in the desert”: The subject, “two vast and trunkless legs of stone,” runs over the line end to its verb, “stand.”


@panel 52

**Inversion and a relative.** “Half sunk, a shattered visage lies, whose frown”: “Near them, on the sand, half sunk” come before the subject, “a shattered visage,” and its verb, “lies.” “Whose” begins a relative clause on “visage.”


@panel 53

**The verb of the relative clause.** “Tell that its sculptor well those passions read”: “Tell” is plural because its subject is three things: “frown, and wrinkled lip, and sneer.” “That” begins a noun clause, and in it the object, “those passions,” comes before the verb “read,” past tense.


@panel 54

**Apposition.** “The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed”: These nouns stand outside the clause and name what survived: the sculptor’s hand that copied the passions and the king’s heart that fed them.


@panel 55

“Who said”

Question: “Who said” is…

Choices:
- A relative clause describing “a traveller”
- A question
- The main clause
- A noun clause, object of “met”

Answer: A relative clause describing “a traveller”

Why: “Who” refers back to the traveler.


@panel 56

“Stand”

Question: The subject of “Stand” is…

Choices:
- “Two vast and trunkless legs of stone”
- “a traveller”
- “the desert”
- “I”

Answer: “Two vast and trunkless legs of stone”

Why: The subject runs over the line end to its verb.


@panel 57

“a shattered visage lies”

Question: In “Near them, on the sand, / Half sunk, a shattered visage lies,” the subject is…

Choices:
- “a shattered visage”
- “the sand”
- “them”
- “Half sunk”

Answer: “a shattered visage”

Why: The phrases of place and state come first; the subject follows.


@panel 58

“Tell”

Question: Why “Tell” and not “Tells”?

Choices:
- Its subject is three things joined by “and”
- It is an imperative
- It goes with “the sculptor”
- It is past tense

Answer: Its subject is three things joined by “and”

Why: “Frown, and wrinkled lip, and sneer” make a plural subject.


@panel 59

“read”

Question: “read” in line 6 is…

Choices:
- Past tense: the sculptor read those passions well
- Present tense
- An infinitive after “tell”
- A noun

Answer: Past tense: the sculptor read those passions well

Why: The object, “those passions,” comes before it, and the sculptor did it long ago.


@panel 60

**Blake, *The Tyger* stanza 1 · Trochaic tetrameter, with the last syllable dropped (in the drill)**

Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

**Context.** From Blake’s *Songs of Experience*, 1794. The lines are trochaic, with the final unstressed syllable cut off, so that each line begins and ends on a stress.


@panel 61

**Address and the beat.** “Tyger Tyger, burning bright”: The tiger is addressed, and “burning bright” describes it. The line scans “TY-ger TY-ger BURN-ing BRIGHT”: three trochees and a stressed syllable.


@panel 62

**A phrase of place.** “In the forests of the night”: “In the forests of the night” says where the tiger burns.


@panel 63

**A question.** “What immortal hand or eye”: “What” asks which hand or eye. “Hand or eye” is the subject of “could frame.”


@panel 64

**The verb and a shifted line.** “Could frame thy fearful symmetry?”: “Could frame” is the verb, and “thy fearful symmetry” the object. This line begins with an unstressed syllable, “could FRAME thy FEAR-ful SYM-me-TRY,” so it turns to iambs.


@panel 65

“Tyger Tyger”

Question: The first line begins with…

Choices:
- A stressed syllable: the line is trochaic
- An unstressed syllable: the line is iambic
- Two unstressed syllables
- A spondee only

Answer: A stressed syllable: the line is trochaic

Why: TY-ger TY-ger BURN-ing BRIGHT.


@panel 66

“burning bright”

Question: “burning bright” describes…

Choices:
- The tiger
- The forests
- The night
- The hand

Answer: The tiger

Why: It follows the address and qualifies it.


@panel 67

“hand or eye”

Question: The subject of “could frame” is…

Choices:
- “hand or eye”
- “thy fearful symmetry”
- “the night”
- “Tyger”

Answer: “hand or eye”

Why: What hand or eye could frame it: the hand or eye does the framing.


@panel 68

“thy fearful symmetry”

Question: “thy fearful symmetry” is…

Choices:
- The object of “could frame”
- The subject
- A noun of address
- An adverb

Answer: The object of “could frame”

Why: It is what the hand or eye frames.


@panel 69

**Pope, *An Essay on Criticism* lines 362–365 · Heroic couplets (in the drill)**

True ease in writing comes from art, not chance,
As those move easiest who have learn’d to dance.
’Tis not enough no harshness gives offence,
The sound must seem an echo to the sense:

**Context.** Pope’s *Essay on Criticism*, 1711, is written in heroic couplets: rhymed pairs of iambic pentameter lines, each pair usually closing its own thought.


@panel 70

**The statement.** “True ease in writing comes from art, not chance”: The subject is “true ease in writing” and the verb “comes.” “Not chance” is set against “art.” Five iambs: “true EASE in WRIT-ing COMES from ART, not CHANCE.”


@panel 71

**A comparison, and a relative clause split from its noun.** “As those move easiest who have learn’d to dance”: “As” begins a clause of comparison. “Who have learn’d to dance” is a relative clause on “those,” put after the verb so that the rhyme falls on “dance.”


@panel 72

**A noun clause without “that”.** “’Tis not enough no harshness gives offence”: “’Tis” is “it is.” “It” looks forward to the clause “no harshness gives offence,” with “that” left out: it is not enough that no harshness offends.


@panel 73

**The rule.** “The sound must seem an echo to the sense”: “Must seem” is the verb, and “an echo to the sense” completes it.


@panel 74

“True ease in writing”

Question: The subject of “comes” is…

Choices:
- “True ease in writing”
- “art”
- “chance”
- “writing” alone

Answer: “True ease in writing”

Why: “In writing” limits “ease”; the whole phrase is the subject.


@panel 75

“who have learn’d to dance”

Question: “who have learn’d to dance” describes…

Choices:
- “those”
- “art”
- “chance”
- “easiest”

Answer: “those”

Why: The relative clause is placed after the verb, but it belongs to “those.”


@panel 76

“’Tis”

Question: In “’Tis not enough no harshness gives offence,” what does “it” point to?

Choices:
- The clause “(that) no harshness gives offence”
- The sound
- Art
- Nothing

Answer: The clause “(that) no harshness gives offence”

Why: “It” is an anticipatory subject; the real subject is the clause that follows, with “that” omitted.


@panel 77

“an echo to the sense”

Question: “an echo to the sense” is…

Choices:
- A complement after “must seem”
- The subject
- The object of “sound”
- An adverb of place

Answer: A complement after “must seem”

Why: “Seem” links the subject to what it is said to be.


@panel 78

**Donne, *Holy Sonnets* X, lines 1–4 · Iambic pentameter, a sonnet (in the drill)**

Death be not proud, though some have called thee
Mighty and dreadful, for, thou art not so,
For, those, whom thou think’st, thou dost overthrow,
Die not, poor death, nor yet canst thou kill me.

**Context.** Donne’s sonnet, printed in 1633, addresses Death and argues with it. Its meter is iambic pentameter, often roughened. The text is Grierson’s, from the edition of 1633, with the spelling modernized; the heavy commas are the old printing’s.


@panel 79

**Address and the older negative imperative.** “Death be not proud”: “Death” is addressed. “Be not proud” is the older form of “do not be proud.”


@panel 80

**A clause of concession.** “though some have called thee
Mighty and dreadful”: “Though” concedes. “Called thee mighty and dreadful”: “thee” is the object, and “mighty and dreadful” say what Death was called.


@panel 81

**The reason.** “for, thou art not so”: “For” gives the reason: you are not so.


@panel 82

**A long subject.** “For, those, whom thou think’st, thou dost overthrow,
Die not”: The subject is “those,” with the relative clause “whom thou think’st thou dost overthrow”; the verb “die not” comes only in the next line. “Whom” is the object of “overthrow,” inside the clause “thou dost overthrow,” which itself depends on “thou think’st.”


@panel 83

**Inversion after “nor”.** “nor yet canst thou kill me”: After “nor” the helping verb comes before the subject: “canst thou.”


@panel 84

“be not proud”

Question: “be not proud” is…

Choices:
- An older form of the negative imperative
- A subjunctive of wish
- A question
- A statement

Answer: An older form of the negative imperative

Why: Older English puts “not” after the imperative: “be not.”


@panel 85

“thee”

Question: In “some have called thee / Mighty and dreadful,” “thee” is…

Choices:
- The object of “called”
- The subject
- A possessive
- A noun of address

Answer: The object of “called”

Why: Some have called Death mighty: “thee” is called something.


@panel 86

“whom”

Question: “whom” is the object of…

Choices:
- “overthrow”
- “think’st”
- “Die”
- “For”

Answer: “overthrow”

Why: Thou think’st [that] thou dost overthrow whom: the relative belongs to the inner clause.


@panel 87

“Die not”

Question: The subject of “Die not” is…

Choices:
- “those”
- “thou”
- “Death”
- “me”

Answer: “those”

Why: Those whom you think you overthrow do not die.


@panel 88

“canst thou”

Question: Why “canst thou” and not “thou canst”?

Choices:
- After “nor” the helping verb comes before the subject
- It is a question
- It is an imperative
- For the rhyme

Answer: After “nor” the helping verb comes before the subject

Why: Negative words at the head of a clause bring inversion: “nor can you.”


@panel 89

**Tennyson, *Ulysses* lines 65–70 · Blank verse (in the drill)**

Tho’ much is taken, much abides; and tho’
We are not now that strength which in old days
Moved earth and heaven; that which we are, we are;
One equal temper of heroic hearts,
Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.

**Context.** The close of Tennyson’s monologue, 1842. The old Ulysses speaks to his mariners in blank verse; the sentence runs over line ends to its last word.


@panel 90

**Concession and statement.** “Tho’ much is taken, much abides”: “Tho’,” Tennyson’s spelling of “though,” concedes: “much is taken”; “much abides” is the main clause. The two “much”s stand against each other.


@panel 91

**A second concession, across the line.** “and tho’
We are not now that strength which in old days
Moved earth and heaven”: The second “tho’” clause runs over the line end. “Which in old days moved earth and heaven” is a relative clause on “that strength.”


@panel 92

**The object placed first.** “that which we are, we are”: “That which we are” stands first for emphasis; the main clause is “we are [that].”


@panel 93

**Apposition.** “One equal temper of heroic hearts”: This phrase renames “that which we are.”


@panel 94

**Participle, adjective and infinitives.** “Made weak by time and fate, but strong in will
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield”: “Made weak” is a past participle, and “strong in will” an adjective phrase; both describe “temper.” The four infinitives complete “will.”


@panel 95

“much abides”

Question: “much abides” is…

Choices:
- The main clause after the concession
- A dependent clause
- A relative clause
- An infinitive phrase

Answer: The main clause after the concession

Why: “Though” governs only “much is taken.”


@panel 96

“which in old days”

Question: “which” refers to…

Choices:
- “that strength”
- “old days”
- “earth and heaven”
- “we”

Answer: “that strength”

Why: The strength that once moved earth and heaven.


@panel 97

“that which we are, we are”

Question: In “that which we are, we are,” the phrase “that which we are” is…

Choices:
- Placed first for emphasis; the clause is “we are that”
- The subject of “are”
- A question
- A dependent clause of time

Answer: Placed first for emphasis; the clause is “we are that”

Why: The complement is moved to the front, and “we are” closes the line.


@panel 98

“Made weak”

Question: “Made weak by time and fate” describes…

Choices:
- “One equal temper of heroic hearts”
- “earth and heaven”
- “old days”
- “will”

Answer: “One equal temper of heroic hearts”

Why: The participle phrase follows the noun phrase it describes.


@panel 99

“To strive”

Question: The infinitives “To strive, to seek, to find” complete…

Choices:
- “will”
- “weak”
- “fate”
- “hearts”

Answer: “will”

Why: Strong in will to strive: they say what the will is for.

EXERCISE — English Poetry: Questions
Five more poems, of Shelley, Blake, Pope, Donne, and Tennyson, each with its construction asked part by part, and then read through.
------------------------------------------------------------------------

@exercise enpoetrydrill
Title: English Poetry: Questions

Five more poems, of Shelley, Blake, Pope, Donne, and Tennyson, each with its construction asked part by part, and then read through.

The exercise begins with two notes. A set ends at 100 points; a right answer adds points and a wrong answer takes some away, and the amount depends on the difficulty chosen on the home screen.

Instruction on the question: Choose the answer about the marked words.

Three examples of each kind of question follow. They are samples, not the whole drill.

#### 1. … … and not …?

2 examples of this kind.

@example 1
id: psg:en-donne:4
difficulty: 1

From: Donne, *Holy Sonnets* X, lines 1–4 · Iambic pentameter, a sonnet

Question: Why “canst thou” and not “thou canst”?

Choices:
- After “nor” the helping verb comes before the subject
- It is an imperative
- It is a question

Answer: After “nor” the helping verb comes before the subject

Why: Negative words at the head of a clause bring inversion: “nor can you.”

difficulty: 1

Passage: I met a traveller from an antique land / Who said: Two vast and trunkless legs of stone / Stand in the desert … Near them, on the sand, / Half sunk, a shattered visage lies, whose frown, / And wrinkled lip, and sneer of cold command, / Tell that its sculptor well those passions read / Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things, / The hand that mocked them, and the heart that fed:

From: Shelley, *Ozymandias* lines 1–8 · Iambic pentameter, a sonnet

Question: “read” in line 6 is…

Choices:
- Present tense
- Past tense: the sculptor read those passions well
- A noun

Answer: Past tense: the sculptor read those passions well

Why: The object, “those passions,” comes before it, and the sculptor did it long ago.


#### 13. … is the object of…

One example of this kind (the whole of it).

@example 1
id: psg:en-donne:2
difficulty: 1

Passage: Death be not proud, though some have called thee / Mighty and dreadful, for, thou art not so, / For, those, whom thou think’st, thou dost overthrow, / Die not, poor death, nor yet canst thou kill me.

From: Donne, *Holy Sonnets* X, lines 1–4 · Iambic pentameter, a sonnet

Question: “whom” is the object of…

Choices:
- “For”
- “overthrow”
- “think’st”

Answer: “overthrow”

Why: Thou think’st [that] thou dost overthrow whom: the relative belongs to the inner clause.


------------------------------------------------------------------------
STUDY — Greek Prose
Fifteen passages of the historians, the philosophers, the orators, and the Gospels, read part by part
------------------------------------------------------------------------

@deck grcprose
Title: Greek Prose
Small heading: Fifteen passages of the historians, the philosophers, the orators, and the Gospels, read part by part
Sources: Smyth

@panel 1

**Herodotus, *Histories* 1.0**

Ἡροδότου Ἁλικαρνησσέος ἱστορίης ἀπόδεξις ἥδε, ὡς μήτε τὰ γενόμενα ἐξ ἀνθρώπων τῷ χρόνῳ ἐξίτηλα γένηται, μήτε ἔργα μεγάλα τε καὶ θωμαστά, τὰ μὲν Ἕλλησι τὰ δὲ βαρβάροισι ἀποδεχθέντα, ἀκλεᾶ γένηται, τά τε ἄλλα καὶ διʼ ἣν αἰτίην ἐπολέμησαν ἀλλήλοισι.

This is the Showing forth of the Inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassos, to the end that neither the deeds of men may be forgotten by lapse of time, nor the works great and marvelous, which have been produced some by Hellenes and some by Barbarians, may lose their renown; and especially that the causes may be remembered for which these waged war with one another.
— G. C. Macaulay

**Context.** Herodotus wrote in the Ionic dialect in the fifth century BC. His history opens with one sentence that names the author, the work, and its purpose: that the deeds of Greeks and barbarians may not be forgotten, and above all the cause of their war.


@panel 2

**A sentence without a verb.** *Ἡροδότου Ἁλικαρνησσέος ἱστορίης ἀπόδεξις ἥδε*: *Ἀπόδεξις ἥδε*, “this is the setting forth,” has no verb: *ἐστί* is understood. *Ἡροδότου Ἁλικαρνησσέος* and *ἱστορίης* are genitives depending on *ἀπόδεξις*. The forms are Ionic: *ἱστορίης* for Attic *ἱστορίας*.


@panel 3

**A purpose clause.** *ὡς μήτε τὰ γενόμενα ἐξ ἀνθρώπων τῷ χρόνῳ ἐξίτηλα γένηται*: *Ὡς* with the subjunctive *γένηται* gives the purpose, and the negative is *μήτε*: so that neither the things done by men may fade with time. *Τὰ γενόμενα*, a participle with the article, is the subject.


@panel 4

**The second subject.** *μήτε ἔργα μεγάλα τε καὶ θωμαστά*: The second *μήτε* brings a second subject, *ἔργα*, “works,” with two adjectives joined by *τε καί*.


@panel 5

**Μέν and δέ.** *τὰ μὲν Ἕλλησι τὰ δὲ βαρβάροισι ἀποδεχθέντα*: *Τὰ μὲν … τὰ δέ* divides the works into two groups, some by Greeks and some by barbarians. *Ἀποδεχθέντα*, an aorist passive participle, agrees with *ἔργα*, and the datives give the agents.


@panel 6

**The second verb.** *ἀκλεᾶ γένηται*: *Ἀκλεᾶ γένηται*, “may become without fame,” is the verb of the second subject, again in the subjunctive of purpose.


@panel 7

**A relative clause of the cause.** *τά τε ἄλλα καὶ διʼ ἣν αἰτίην ἐπολέμησαν ἀλλήλοισι*: *Τά τε ἄλλα καί* means “both the rest and especially.” *Διʼ ἣν αἰτίην*, “for what cause,” begins a clause whose antecedent is drawn into it, and *ἐπολέμησαν* is aorist.


@panel 8

*ἀπόδεξις ἥδε*

Question: What verb must be supplied in *ἀπόδεξις ἥδε*?

Choices:
- *ἐστί*, “is”
- *γράφει*, “writes”
- *ἦν*, “was”
- None, because the clause is a vocative

Answer: *ἐστί*, “is”

Why: Greek often leaves out the present of “be.” The sentence means: this is the setting forth.


@panel 9

*ὡς μήτε*

Question: *ὡς … γένηται* is…

Choices:
- A purpose clause with the subjunctive
- A result clause with the indicative
- A comparison: “as … happens”
- A temporal clause: “when … happened”

Answer: A purpose clause with the subjunctive

Why: *Ὡς* with the subjunctive and the negative *μή* gives the purpose of the setting forth.


@panel 10

*τὰ μὲν Ἕλλησι τὰ δὲ βαρβάροισι*

Question: *τὰ μὲν … τὰ δέ* does what?

Choices:
- Divides the works into two groups: some … others
- Joins two verbs
- Marks a question
- Gives a cause

Answer: Divides the works into two groups: some … others

Why: *Μέν* and *δέ* set the two halves against each other: some by Greeks, others by barbarians.


@panel 11

*ἀποδεχθέντα*

Question: *ἀποδεχθέντα* is…

Choices:
- An aorist passive participle agreeing with *ἔργα*
- A finite verb in the aorist
- An infinitive
- A present active participle

Answer: An aorist passive participle agreeing with *ἔργα*

Why: The ending *-θέντα* marks the aorist passive participle, neuter plural like *ἔργα*.


@panel 12

*ἐπολέμησαν*

Question: *ἐπολέμησαν* is…

Choices:
- Aorist indicative, third person plural: “they made war”
- Imperfect
- Present subjunctive
- Future

Answer: Aorist indicative, third person plural: “they made war”

Why: The augment *ἐ-* and the ending *-σαν* mark the aorist.


@panel 13

**Thucydides, *History* 1.1.1**

Θουκυδίδης Ἀθηναῖος ξυνέγραψε τὸν πόλεμον τῶν Πελοποννησίων καὶ Ἀθηναίων, ὡς ἐπολέμησαν πρὸς ἀλλήλους, ἀρξάμενος εὐθὺς καθισταμένου καὶ ἐλπίσας μέγαν τε ἔσεσθαι καὶ ἀξιολογώτατον τῶν προγεγενημένων, τεκμαιρόμενος ὅτι ἀκμάζοντές τε ᾖσαν ἐς αὐτὸν ἀμφότεροι παρασκευῇ τῇ πάσῃ καὶ τὸ ἄλλο Ἑλληνικὸν ὁρῶν ξυνιστάμενον πρὸς ἑκατέρους, τὸ μὲν εὐθύς, τὸ δὲ καὶ διανοούμενον.

Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, beginning at the moment that it broke out, and believing that it would be a great war and more worthy of relation than any that had preceded it. This belief was not without its grounds. The preparations of both the combatants were in every department in the last state of perfection; and he could see the rest of the Hellenic race taking sides in the quarrel; those who delayed doing so at once having it in contemplation.
— Richard Crawley

**Context.** Thucydides opens his history of the war between Athens and Sparta (431–404 BC) by naming himself and his subject, and by saying why he began to write at once. The sentence has one main verb and a chain of participles.


@panel 14

**The main clause.** *Θουκυδίδης Ἀθηναῖος ξυνέγραψε τὸν πόλεμον τῶν Πελοποννησίων καὶ Ἀθηναίων*: The subject is *Θουκυδίδης*, the verb *ξυνέγραψε* (aorist, “wrote up”), and the object *τὸν πόλεμον*. Thucydides writes *ξυν-* for Attic *συν-*.


@panel 15

**An indirect question.** *ὡς ἐπολέμησαν πρὸς ἀλλήλους*: *Ὡς*, “how,” introduces how they made war against one another.


@panel 16

**A participle and a genitive absolute.** *ἀρξάμενος εὐθὺς καθισταμένου*: *Ἀρξάμενος*, an aorist middle participle, agrees with Thucydides: having begun. *Καθισταμένου* is a genitive absolute with the war understood: as soon as it was arising.


@panel 17

**A participle with a future infinitive.** *καὶ ἐλπίσας μέγαν τε ἔσεσθαι καὶ ἀξιολογώτατον τῶν προγεγενημένων*: *Ἐλπίσας*, “expecting,” takes the future infinitive *ἔσεσθαι*: that it would be great and the most worth telling. *Τῶν προγεγενημένων* is a genitive with the superlative: of those before.


@panel 18

**A third participle.** *τεκμαιρόμενος ὅτι ἀκμάζοντές τε ᾖσαν ἐς αὐτὸν ἀμφότεροι παρασκευῇ τῇ πάσῃ*: *Τεκμαιρόμενος*, “judging,” takes a clause with *ὅτι*: that both sides came to it at their height in every preparation. *Ἦισαν* is the imperfect of *εἶμι*, “go.”


@panel 19

**A participle after a verb of seeing.** *καὶ τὸ ἄλλο Ἑλληνικὸν ὁρῶν ξυνιστάμενον πρὸς ἑκατέρους*: *Ὁρῶν*, “seeing,” takes the participle *ξυνιστάμενον*: seeing the rest of Greece siding with one side or the other.


@panel 20

*ξυνέγραψε*

Question: What is the main verb?

Choices:
- *ξυνέγραψε*, “wrote up”
- *ἐπολέμησαν*
- *ἀρξάμενος*
- *ἔσεσθαι*

Answer: *ξυνέγραψε*, “wrote up”

Why: *Ἐπολέμησαν* belongs to a dependent clause, and the others are a participle and an infinitive.


@panel 21

*ἀρξάμενος*

Question: *ἀρξάμενος* agrees with…

Choices:
- *Θουκυδίδης*, the subject
- *τὸν πόλεμον*
- *Ἀθηναίων*
- *ἀλλήλους*

Answer: *Θουκυδίδης*, the subject

Why: It is nominative masculine singular, like the subject.


@panel 22

*καθισταμένου*

Question: *καθισταμένου* is…

Choices:
- A genitive absolute with the war understood: as it was arising
- A genitive of possession with *πόλεμον*
- The object of *ἀρξάμενος* alone
- A finite verb

Answer: A genitive absolute with the war understood: as it was arising

Why: A participle in the genitive, standing apart, gives the time; the noun, the war, is understood from before.


@panel 23

*ἔσεσθαι*

Question: *ἔσεσθαι* is…

Choices:
- A future infinitive after *ἐλπίσας*
- A present infinitive
- An aorist indicative
- A participle

Answer: A future infinitive after *ἐλπίσας*

Why: Verbs of hoping and expecting take the future infinitive.


@panel 24

*ὁρῶν*

Question: *ὁρῶν … ξυνιστάμενον* shows…

Choices:
- A verb of seeing with a participle: seeing it take sides
- A purpose clause
- A genitive absolute
- An infinitive of result

Answer: A verb of seeing with a participle: seeing it take sides

Why: Verbs of perceiving take a participle that agrees with the thing perceived.


@panel 25

**Thucydides, *History* 1.22.4**

καὶ ἐς μὲν ἀκρόασιν ἴσως τὸ μὴ μυθῶδες αὐτῶν ἀτερπέστερον φανεῖται· ὅσοι δὲ βουλήσονται τῶν τε γενομένων τὸ σαφὲς σκοπεῖν καὶ τῶν μελλόντων ποτὲ αὖθις κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον τοιούτων καὶ παραπλησίων ἔσεσθαι, ὠφέλιμα κρίνειν αὐτὰ ἀρκούντως ἕξει. κτῆμά τε ἐς αἰεὶ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀγώνισμα ἐς τὸ παραχρῆμα ἀκούειν ξύγκειται.

The absence of romance in my history will, I fear, detract somewhat from its interest; but if it be judged useful by those inquirers who desire an exact knowledge of the past as an aid to the interpretation of the future, which in the course of human things must resemble if it does not reflect it, I shall be content. In fine, I have written my work, not as an essay which is to win the applause of the moment, but as a possession for all time.
— Richard Crawley

**Context.** In his account of his method, Thucydides says what kind of reader his history is for. Crawley’s English is free here, and the Latin of the Greek is close.


@panel 26

**The first member.** *καὶ ἐς μὲν ἀκρόασιν ἴσως τὸ μὴ μυθῶδες αὐτῶν ἀτερπέστερον φανεῖται*: *Τὸ μὴ μυθῶδες*, an adjective made a noun by the article, is the subject: the absence of the fabulous. *Ἀτερπέστερον* is a comparative, and *φανεῖται* is future. *Μέν* prepares the contrast.


@panel 27

**The second member.** *ὅσοι δὲ βουλήσονται*: *Δέ* answers *μέν*. *Ὅσοι*, “as many as,” begins a relative clause that serves as the subject of the main verb.


@panel 28

**The object of their wish.** *τῶν τε γενομένων τὸ σαφὲς σκοπεῖν*: *Σκοπεῖν*, “to look at,” completes *βουλήσονται*, and *τὸ σαφές*, “the clear truth,” is its object, with the genitive *τῶν γενομένων*: of what happened.


@panel 29

**Things to come.** *καὶ τῶν μελλόντων ποτὲ αὖθις κατὰ τὸ ἀνθρώπινον τοιούτων καὶ παραπλησίων ἔσεσθαι*: A second genitive: of the things that will, as human nature goes, be such and similar again.


@panel 30

**The main verb, impersonal.** *ὠφέλιμα κρίνειν αὐτὰ ἀρκούντως ἕξει*: *Ἀρκούντως ἕξει*, “it will be enough,” has the infinitive *κρίνειν*: if they judge the work useful. *Ἔχω* with an adverb means “be in a state.”


@panel 31

**The famous sentence.** *κτῆμά τε ἐς αἰεὶ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀγώνισμα ἐς τὸ παραχρῆμα ἀκούειν ξύγκειται*: *Ξύγκειται*, “it is composed,” is the verb; *κτῆμα ἐς αἰεί*, “a possession for ever,” is set against *ἀγώνισμα ἐς τὸ παραχρῆμα*, “a prize piece for the moment,” by *μᾶλλον ἤ*.


@panel 32

*τὸ μὴ μυθῶδες*

Question: *τὸ μὴ μυθῶδες* is…

Choices:
- An adjective made a noun by the article: the absence of the fabulous
- A finite verb
- A genitive of comparison
- A purpose clause

Answer: An adjective made a noun by the article: the absence of the fabulous

Why: The neuter article makes the adjective a noun, and *μή* negates it.


@panel 33

*φανεῖται*

Question: *φανεῖται* is…

Choices:
- Future: “will appear”
- Present: “appears”
- Aorist
- Imperfect

Answer: Future: “will appear”

Why: The contracted future of *φαίνομαι*.


@panel 34

*ὅσοι δὲ βουλήσονται*

Question: *ὅσοι … βουλήσονται* is…

Choices:
- A relative clause standing as the subject of the thought
- A purpose clause
- A genitive absolute
- An indirect question

Answer: A relative clause standing as the subject of the thought

Why: *Ὅσοι*, “as many as,” names those for whom the work will be useful.


@panel 35

*ἀρκούντως ἕξει*

Question: *ἀρκούντως ἕξει* means…

Choices:
- “It will be enough”: *ἔχω* with an adverb
- “He will have enough”
- “It has been enough”
- “They will hold sufficiently”

Answer: “It will be enough”: *ἔχω* with an adverb

Why: *Ἔχω* with an adverb describes a state: it will be well enough.


@panel 36

*μᾶλλον ἢ*

Question: *μᾶλλον ἢ* sets what against what?

Choices:
- A possession for ever against a prize piece for the moment
- Hearing against reading
- The Greeks against the barbarians
- The past against the future

Answer: A possession for ever against a prize piece for the moment

Why: The comparison names the two kinds of work.


@panel 37

**Plato, *Apology* 17a**

ὅτι μὲν ὑμεῖς, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, πεπόνθατε ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν κατηγόρων, οὐκ οἶδα· ἐγὼ δʼ οὖν καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπʼ αὐτῶν ὀλίγου ἐμαυτοῦ ἐπελαθόμην, οὕτω πιθανῶς ἔλεγον. καίτοι ἀληθές γε ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν οὐδὲν εἰρήκασιν.

How you, O Athenians, have been affected by my accusers, I cannot tell; but I know that they almost made me forget who I was, so persuasively did they speak; and yet they have hardly uttered a word of truth.
— Benjamin Jowett

**Context.** Socrates begins his defense before the Athenian jury in 399 BC. He sets his own experience of the accusers’ speeches against what the jury may have felt.


@panel 38

**An indirect question placed first.** *ὅτι μὲν ὑμεῖς, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, πεπόνθατε ὑπὸ τῶν ἐμῶν κατηγόρων*: *Ὅτι* here means “what” (*ὅ τι*): what you have felt. The clause is the object of *οἶδα*, held first. *Ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι* is the usual address to the jury.


@panel 39

**The main verb.** *οὐκ οἶδα*: *Οἶδα*, “I know,” is a perfect form with a present meaning.


@panel 40

**The contrast.** *ἐγὼ δʼ οὖν καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπʼ αὐτῶν ὀλίγου ἐμαυτοῦ ἐπελαθόμην*: *Δέ* answers *μέν*. *Ἐπελαθόμην*, “I forgot,” takes the genitive *ἐμαυτοῦ*, and *ὀλίγου* means “almost.”


@panel 41

**A clause of degree.** *οὕτω πιθανῶς ἔλεγον*: *Οὕτω πιθανῶς ἔλεγον*, “so persuasively did they speak,” gives the reason, set beside the rest without a conjunction.


@panel 42

**The turn.** *καίτοι ἀληθές γε ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν οὐδὲν εἰρήκασιν*: *Καίτοι*, “and yet,” turns the thought. *Ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν*, “so to speak,” softens *οὐδέν*, and *εἰρήκασιν* is perfect.


@panel 43

*ὅτι μὲν ὑμεῖς*

Question: *ὅτι … πεπόνθατε* is…

Choices:
- An indirect question, the object of *οἶδα*
- A causal clause
- A purpose clause
- The main clause

Answer: An indirect question, the object of *οἶδα*

Why: What the jury has felt is the thing Socrates does not know.


@panel 44

*ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι*

Question: *ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι* is…

Choices:
- Vocative: the address to the jury
- Nominative subject
- Genitive
- Dative

Answer: Vocative: the address to the jury

Why: *Ὦ* with the vocative is the regular address.


@panel 45

*ἐμαυτοῦ*

Question: Why is *ἐμαυτοῦ* genitive?

Choices:
- *ἐπιλανθάνομαι*, “forget,” takes the genitive
- It is a genitive absolute
- It shows possession of *αὐτῶν*
- It follows *ὑπό*

Answer: *ἐπιλανθάνομαι*, “forget,” takes the genitive

Why: Verbs of remembering and forgetting take the genitive.


@panel 46

*εἰρήκασιν*

Question: *εἰρήκασιν* is…

Choices:
- Perfect, third person plural: “they have said”
- Aorist
- Future
- Present

Answer: Perfect, third person plural: “they have said”

Why: The reduplicated stem *εἰρη-* and *-κασι* mark the perfect active.


@panel 47

**Plato, *Republic* 327a**

κατέβην χθὲς εἰς Πειραιᾶ μετὰ Γλαύκωνος τοῦ Ἀρίστωνος προσευξόμενός τε τῇ θεῷ καὶ ἅμα τὴν ἑορτὴν βουλόμενος θεάσασθαι τίνα τρόπον ποιήσουσιν ἅτε νῦν πρῶτον ἄγοντες.

I went down yesterday to the Piraeus with Glaucon the son of Ariston, that I might offer up my prayers to the goddess; and also because I wanted to see in what manner they would celebrate the festival, which was a new thing.
— Benjamin Jowett

**Context.** Socrates tells how the conversation of the Republic came about. He had gone down to the harbor of Athens for a new festival of a Thracian goddess.


@panel 48

**The main verb.** *κατέβην χθὲς εἰς Πειραιᾶ*: *Κατέβην* is the aorist of *καταβαίνω*, “I went down,” and *εἰς Πειραιᾶ* gives the place to which.


@panel 49

**Μετά with the genitive.** *μετὰ Γλαύκωνος τοῦ Ἀρίστωνος*: *Μετά* with the genitive means “with.” *Τοῦ Ἀρίστωνος*, with “son” understood, names his father.


@panel 50

**A future participle of purpose.** *προσευξόμενός τε τῇ θεῷ*: *Προσευξόμενος*, a future participle, gives the purpose: to pray to the goddess. *Τῇ θεῷ* is dative with the verb of praying.


@panel 51

**A present participle of cause.** *καὶ ἅμα τὴν ἑορτὴν βουλόμενος θεάσασθαι*: *Βουλόμενος*, “wishing,” gives a second reason, and *θεάσασθαι* is the aorist infinitive it governs.


@panel 52

**An indirect question.** *τίνα τρόπον ποιήσουσιν ἅτε νῦν πρῶτον ἄγοντες*: *Τίνα τρόπον*, “in what way,” begins an indirect question with the future *ποιήσουσιν*. *Ἅτε … ἄγοντες*, “since they were holding it now for the first time,” gives a reason as a fact.


@panel 53

*κατέβην*

Question: *κατέβην* is…

Choices:
- Aorist, first person singular: “I went down”
- Imperfect
- Present
- Perfect

Answer: Aorist, first person singular: “I went down”

Why: *Ἔβην* is the root aorist of *βαίνω*, here compounded with *κατα-*.


@panel 54

*μετὰ Γλαύκωνος*

Question: *μετὰ Γλαύκωνος* means…

Choices:
- “With Glaucon”: *μετά* with the genitive
- “After Glaucon”
- “Among Glaucon”
- “Toward Glaucon”

Answer: “With Glaucon”: *μετά* with the genitive

Why: With the genitive, *μετά* means “with”; with the accusative, “after.”


@panel 55

*προσευξόμενός*

Question: *προσευξόμενος* expresses…

Choices:
- Purpose, as a future participle
- Past time
- Concession
- Condition

Answer: Purpose, as a future participle

Why: A future participle after a verb of motion gives the purpose.


@panel 56

*τίνα τρόπον*

Question: *τίνα τρόπον ποιήσουσιν* is…

Choices:
- An indirect question after *θεάσασθαι*
- A relative clause
- A main clause
- A purpose clause

Answer: An indirect question after *θεάσασθαι*

Why: *Τίνα*, “what,” asks the question that Socrates wished to see answered.


@panel 57

**Xenophon, *Anabasis* 1.1.1**

Δαρείου καὶ Παρυσάτιδος γίγνονται παῖδες δύο, πρεσβύτερος μὲν Ἀρταξέρξης, νεώτερος δὲ Κῦρος· ἐπεὶ δὲ ἠσθένει Δαρεῖος καὶ ὑπώπτευε τελευτὴν τοῦ βίου, ἐβούλετο τὼ παῖδε ἀμφοτέρω παρεῖναι.

Darius and Parysatis had two sons: the elder was named Artaxerxes, and the younger Cyrus. Now, as Darius lay sick and felt that the end of life drew near, he wished both his sons to be with him.
— H. G. Dakyns

**Context.** Xenophon’s Anabasis tells of the march of the younger Cyrus against his brother, the king of Persia, and of the return of the Greek soldiers. It begins plainly, with the family of the king.


@panel 58

**The historical present.** *Δαρείου καὶ Παρυσάτιδος γίγνονται παῖδες δύο*: *Γίγνονται*, “are born,” is the historical present, used for a past event in narrative. The genitives name the parents: of Darius and Parysatis.


@panel 59

**Μέν and δέ.** *πρεσβύτερος μὲν Ἀρταξέρξης, νεώτερος δὲ Κῦρος*: *Μὲν … δέ* divides the two sons, the elder and the younger, with “was” understood.


@panel 60

**A clause of time.** *ἐπεὶ δὲ ἠσθένει Δαρεῖος καὶ ὑπώπτευε τελευτὴν τοῦ βίου*: *Ἐπεί*, “when,” begins a clause with two imperfects: he was sick and suspected the end of his life.


@panel 61

**The dual.** *ἐβούλετο τὼ παῖδε ἀμφοτέρω παρεῖναι*: *Τὼ παῖδε ἀμφοτέρω* is the dual, the number for two, as the subject of the infinitive *παρεῖναι*: he wished both sons to be present.


@panel 62

*Δαρείου καὶ Παρυσάτιδος*

Question: *Δαρείου καὶ Παρυσάτιδος* is…

Choices:
- Genitive of origin: born of Darius and Parysatis
- A genitive absolute
- The subject
- A dative

Answer: Genitive of origin: born of Darius and Parysatis

Why: The genitive names the parents from whom the sons are born.


@panel 63

*γίγνονται*

Question: Why is *γίγνονται* present?

Choices:
- It is the historical present, used in narrative for a past event
- The sons are still being born
- It is a future
- It is a mistake for the aorist

Answer: It is the historical present, used in narrative for a past event

Why: Greek narrative often uses the present to make a past event vivid.


@panel 64

*ἠσθένει*

Question: *ἠσθένει* is…

Choices:
- Imperfect: “he was sick”
- Aorist
- Present
- Future

Answer: Imperfect: “he was sick”

Why: The augment and the ending *-ει* of a contract verb in *-έω* mark the imperfect.


@panel 65

*τὼ παῖδε ἀμφοτέρω*

Question: *τὼ παῖδε ἀμφοτέρω* is in which number?

Choices:
- The dual
- The singular
- The plural
- None, it is indeclinable

Answer: The dual

Why: Greek has a dual for pairs, with the endings *-ω* and *-ε*.


@panel 66

**Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* 1094a1–3**

πᾶσα τέχνη καὶ πᾶσα μέθοδος, ὁμοίως δὲ πρᾶξίς τε καὶ προαίρεσις, ἀγαθοῦ τινὸς ἐφίεσθαι δοκεῖ· διὸ καλῶς ἀπεφήναντο τἀγαθόν, οὗ πάντʼ ἐφίεται.

Every art, and every science reduced to a teachable form, and in like manner every action and moral choice, aims, it is thought, at some good: for which reason a common and by no means a bad description of the Chief Good is, “that which all things aim at.”
— D. P. Chase

**Context.** Aristotle opens the Ethics with a claim about all human activity, and draws from it a definition of the good. The sentence has four subjects and one verb.


@panel 67

**Four subjects.** *πᾶσα τέχνη καὶ πᾶσα μέθοδος, ὁμοίως δὲ πρᾶξίς τε καὶ προαίρεσις*: Four nouns are the subject: every art and every inquiry, and likewise action and choice.


@panel 68

**The verb.** *ἀγαθοῦ τινὸς ἐφίεσθαι δοκεῖ*: *Δοκεῖ*, “seems,” is singular, agreeing with the nearest subject, and takes the infinitive *ἐφίεσθαι*, “to aim at,” which governs the genitive *ἀγαθοῦ τινος*.


@panel 69

**The conclusion.** *διὸ καλῶς ἀπεφήναντο τἀγαθόν*: *Διό*, “therefore,” draws the conclusion. *Τἀγαθόν* is *τὸ ἀγαθόν* joined into one word (crasis), the object of *ἀπεφήναντο*.


@panel 70

**A relative clause.** *οὗ πάντʼ ἐφίεται*: *Οὗ*, a genitive relative, is governed by *ἐφίεται*: that at which all things aim. *Πάντʼ* is *πάντα* with its last vowel elided, and a neuter plural takes a singular verb.


@panel 71

*ἀγαθοῦ τινὸς*

Question: Why is *ἀγαθοῦ τινος* genitive?

Choices:
- *ἐφίεμαι*, “aim at,” takes the genitive
- It shows possession
- It is a genitive absolute
- It follows *δοκεῖ*

Answer: *ἐφίεμαι*, “aim at,” takes the genitive

Why: Verbs of aiming and desiring take the genitive.


@panel 72

*δοκεῖ*

Question: Why is *δοκεῖ* singular with four subjects?

Choices:
- It agrees with the nearest subject
- The subjects are one thing
- It is impersonal and has no subject
- It is a mistake

Answer: It agrees with the nearest subject

Why: Greek may make the verb agree with the nearest of several subjects.


@panel 73

*τἀγαθόν*

Question: *τἀγαθόν* is…

Choices:
- *τὸ ἀγαθόν* joined by crasis
- A genitive plural
- A verb
- A participle

Answer: *τὸ ἀγαθόν* joined by crasis

Why: Crasis merges a final vowel with the vowel that begins the next word.


@panel 74

*ἐφίεται*

Question: Why is *ἐφίεται* singular with *πάντα*?

Choices:
- A neuter plural subject takes a singular verb
- *πάντα* is singular
- The verb is impersonal
- It agrees with *οὗ*

Answer: A neuter plural subject takes a singular verb

Why: In Attic, a neuter plural subject usually has its verb in the singular.


@panel 75

**Aristotle, *Politics* 1252a1–7**

ἐπειδὴ πᾶσαν πόλιν ὁρῶμεν κοινωνίαν τινὰ οὖσαν καὶ πᾶσαν κοινωνίαν ἀγαθοῦ τινος ἕνεκεν συνεστηκυῖαν (τοῦ γὰρ εἶναι δοκοῦντος ἀγαθοῦ χάριν πάντα πράττουσι πάντες), δῆλον ὡς πᾶσαι μὲν ἀγαθοῦ τινος στοχάζονται, μάλιστα δὲ καὶ τοῦ κυριωτάτου πάντων ἡ πασῶν κυριωτάτη καὶ πάσας περιέχουσα τὰς ἄλλας.

As we see that every city is a society, and every society is established for some good purpose; for an apparent good is the spring of all human actions; it is evident that this is the principle upon which they are every one founded, and this is more especially true of that which has for its object the best possible, and is itself the most excellent, and comprehends all the rest.
— William Ellis

**Context.** Aristotle begins the Politics, as he begins the Ethics, with the good at which things aim. The city is the society that aims at the highest good.


@panel 76

**A clause of cause with a participle.** *ἐπειδὴ πᾶσαν πόλιν ὁρῶμεν κοινωνίαν τινὰ οὖσαν*: *Ἐπειδή*, “since,” gives the ground. *Ὁρῶμεν* takes the participle *οὖσαν*: we see that every city is a community.


@panel 77

**A second participle.** *καὶ πᾶσαν κοινωνίαν ἀγαθοῦ τινος ἕνεκεν συνεστηκυῖαν*: *Συνεστηκυῖαν*, a perfect participle, depends on *ὁρῶμεν* in the same way. *Ἕνεκεν*, “for the sake of,” follows its genitive.


@panel 78

**A parenthesis.** *(τοῦ γὰρ εἶναι δοκοῦντος ἀγαθοῦ χάριν πάντα πράττουσι πάντες)*: *Χάριν*, like *ἕνεκεν*, follows its genitive: for the sake of what seems good, all do all things.


@panel 79

**The main clause.** *δῆλον ὡς πᾶσαι μὲν ἀγαθοῦ τινος στοχάζονται*: *Δῆλον* (*ἐστί*) is the main clause, “it is clear,” and *ὡς* introduces what is clear.


@panel 80

**Superlatives.** *μάλιστα δὲ καὶ τοῦ κυριωτάτου πάντων ἡ πασῶν κυριωτάτη*: *Ἡ πασῶν κυριωτάτη*, “the most authoritative of all,” is the subject, aiming at the most authoritative good.


@panel 81

*ἐπειδὴ*

Question: *ἐπειδὴ … ὁρῶμεν* is…

Choices:
- A causal clause: since we see
- A purpose clause
- A condition
- The main clause

Answer: A causal clause: since we see

Why: *Ἐπειδή* gives the ground for what is clear.


@panel 82

*οὖσαν*

Question: *οὖσαν* after *ὁρῶμεν* shows…

Choices:
- A verb of seeing with a participle
- A genitive absolute
- An infinitive
- A future

Answer: A verb of seeing with a participle

Why: Verbs of perceiving take a participle agreeing with the thing perceived.


@panel 83

*ἕνεκεν*

Question: *ἕνεκεν* governs…

Choices:
- The genitive, which comes before it
- The dative
- The accusative
- Nothing

Answer: The genitive, which comes before it

Why: *Ἕνεκα* and *χάριν* follow the genitive they govern.


@panel 84

*δῆλον*

Question: What is the main clause?

Choices:
- *δῆλον*, with *ἐστί* understood: “it is clear”
- *ὁρῶμεν*
- *πράττουσι*
- *στοχάζονται*

Answer: *δῆλον*, with *ἐστί* understood: “it is clear”

Why: The other verbs belong to dependent clauses or to the parenthesis.


@panel 85

**The Gospel according to John, ** 1:1–5**

Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, καὶ ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος. οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν. πάντα διʼ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο, καὶ χωρὶς αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο οὐδὲ ἕν. ὃ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν, καὶ ἡ ζωὴ ἦν τὸ φῶς τῶν ἀνθρώπων· καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει, καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life; and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
— King James Version

**Context.** The Gospel of John opens with a prologue on the Word. The clauses are short and joined by καί. The edition punctuates verse 3 so that ὃ γέγονεν begins a new sentence, whereas the King James Version joins it to the sentence before.


@panel 86

**The imperfect of being.** *Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος*: *Ἦν*, the imperfect of *εἰμί*, says what already was in the beginning. *Ὁ λόγος* is the subject.


@panel 87

**The predicate without the article.** *καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος*: *Ὁ λόγος* has the article and is the subject; *θεός* without the article, placed first, is the predicate.


@panel 88

**The aorist of becoming.** *πάντα διʼ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο*: *Ἐγένετο*, the aorist of *γίγνομαι*, “came to be.” *Διʼ αὐτοῦ*, with the genitive, means “through him.”


@panel 89

**A relative clause as subject.** *ὃ γέγονεν ἐν αὐτῷ ζωὴ ἦν*: *Ὃ γέγονεν*, “what has come to be,” is a relative clause with a perfect verb, and in this punctuation it is the subject: what has come to be was life in him.


@panel 90

**The aorist.** *καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν*: *Κατέλαβεν* is aorist, and *αὐτό*, neuter, refers to *τὸ φῶς*.


@panel 91

*ἦν ὁ λόγος*

Question: *ἦν* is…

Choices:
- Imperfect of *εἰμί*: “was”
- Aorist of *γίγνομαι*
- Present
- Future

Answer: Imperfect of *εἰμί*: “was”

Why: *Ἦν* is the imperfect, “was,” of a continuing state.


@panel 92

*θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος*

Question: In *θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος*, which word is the subject?

Choices:
- *ὁ λόγος*, which has the article
- *θεός*, which stands first
- Neither: the sentence has no subject
- *ἦν*

Answer: *ὁ λόγος*, which has the article

Why: The noun with the article is the subject, and the one without it is the predicate.


@panel 93

*διʼ αὐτοῦ*

Question: *διʼ αὐτοῦ* means…

Choices:
- “Through him”: *διά* with the genitive
- “Because of him”: *διά* with the accusative
- “Against him”
- “Before him”

Answer: “Through him”: *διά* with the genitive

Why: *Διά* with the genitive gives the means; with the accusative, the cause.


@panel 94

*ὃ γέγονεν*

Question: *γέγονεν* is…

Choices:
- Perfect: “has come to be”
- Aorist
- Imperfect
- Present

Answer: Perfect: “has come to be”

Why: The reduplicated stem *γε-γον-* marks the perfect.


@panel 95

*αὐτὸ*

Question: *αὐτό* refers to…

Choices:
- *τὸ φῶς*, the light
- *ἡ σκοτία*
- *ὁ λόγος*
- *ἡ ζωή*

Answer: *τὸ φῶς*, the light

Why: *Αὐτό* is neuter, like *τὸ φῶς*.


@panel 96

**Plato, *Phaedo* 118a**

ὦ Κρίτων, ἔφη, τῷ Ἀσκληπιῷ ὀφείλομεν ἀλεκτρυόνα· ἀλλὰ ἀπόδοτε καὶ μὴ ἀμελήσητε.

Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?
— Benjamin Jowett

**Context.** These are the last words of Socrates, as Phaedo reports them, after he has drunk the hemlock. Jowett’s English turns the command into a question.


@panel 97

**The address and the verb of saying.** *ὦ Κρίτων, ἔφη*: *Ὦ Κρίτων* is the vocative, and *ἔφη*, “he said,” is set inside the quoted words.


@panel 98

**A dative and an accusative.** *τῷ Ἀσκληπιῷ ὀφείλομεν ἀλεκτρυόνα*: *Ὀφείλομεν*, “we owe,” takes the thing owed in the accusative, *ἀλεκτρυόνα*, and the one to whom it is owed in the dative.


@panel 99

**An aorist imperative.** *ἀλλὰ ἀπόδοτε*: *Ἀπόδοτε*, “pay back,” is an aorist imperative, plural: a command to do it once.


@panel 100

**A prohibition.** *καὶ μὴ ἀμελήσητε*: *Μή* with the aorist subjunctive is the regular way to forbid an act: do not neglect it.


@panel 101

*τῷ Ἀσκληπιῷ*

Question: *τῷ Ἀσκληπιῷ* is…

Choices:
- Dative: the one to whom the debt is owed
- Genitive
- Accusative
- Vocative

Answer: Dative: the one to whom the debt is owed

Why: The person to whom something is owed stands in the dative.


@panel 102

*ὀφείλομεν*

Question: Why is *ὀφείλομεν* plural?

Choices:
- Socrates speaks for himself and his friends: “we owe”
- It agrees with *Ἀσκληπιῷ*
- It is a mistake for the singular
- It is a passive

Answer: Socrates speaks for himself and his friends: “we owe”

Why: The ending *-ομεν* marks the first person plural.


@panel 103

*ἀπόδοτε*

Question: *ἀπόδοτε* is…

Choices:
- An aorist imperative, second person plural
- A present indicative
- An aorist indicative
- An infinitive

Answer: An aorist imperative, second person plural

Why: *Ἀπόδοτε* is the aorist imperative of *ἀποδίδωμι*.


@panel 104

*μὴ ἀμελήσητε*

Question: *μὴ ἀμελήσητε* is…

Choices:
- A prohibition: *μή* with the aorist subjunctive
- A purpose clause
- A condition
- A fear clause

Answer: A prohibition: *μή* with the aorist subjunctive

Why: Greek forbids a single act with *μή* and the aorist subjunctive.


@panel 105

**Thucydides, *History* 2.35.1 (in the drill)**

οἱ μὲν πολλοὶ τῶν ἐνθάδε ἤδη εἰρηκότων ἐπαινοῦσι τὸν προσθέντα τῷ νόμῳ τὸν λόγον τόνδε, ὡς καλὸν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐκ τῶν πολέμων θαπτομένοις ἀγορεύεσθαι αὐτόν.

Most of my predecessors in this place have commended him who made this speech part of the law, telling us that it is well that it should be delivered at the burial of those who fall in battle.
— Richard Crawley

**Context.** Pericles begins the funeral oration for the Athenians who died in the first year of the war (431 BC). He starts from the custom of the speech itself.


@panel 106

**The subject.** *οἱ μὲν πολλοὶ τῶν ἐνθάδε ἤδη εἰρηκότων*: *Οἱ πολλοί*, “the many,” is the subject, with a partitive genitive: of those who have already spoken here. *Εἰρηκότων* is a perfect participle.


@panel 107

**The verb and its object.** *ἐπαινοῦσι τὸν προσθέντα τῷ νόμῳ τὸν λόγον τόνδε*: *Ἐπαινοῦσι*, “praise,” has as its object *τὸν προσθέντα*, the one who added this speech to the law.


@panel 108

**The reason given.** *ὡς καλὸν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐκ τῶν πολέμων θαπτομένοις ἀγορεύεσθαι αὐτόν*: *Ὡς* gives the reason they offer: that it is good for it to be spoken over those buried from the wars. *Ἀγορεύεσθαι* is a passive infinitive with *αὐτόν*, the speech, as its subject.


@panel 109

*εἰρηκότων*

Question: *εἰρηκότων* is…

Choices:
- A perfect participle, genitive plural
- An aorist indicative
- A present infinitive
- A future participle

Answer: A perfect participle, genitive plural

Why: The reduplicated perfect stem with *-κότων*: of those who have spoken.


@panel 110

*τὸν προσθέντα*

Question: *τὸν προσθέντα* means…

Choices:
- “The one who added”: an aorist participle with the article
- “The law”
- “The speech”
- “They added”

Answer: “The one who added”: an aorist participle with the article

Why: The article makes the participle a noun: the man who added the speech to the law.


@panel 111

*τῷ νόμῳ*

Question: *τῷ νόμῳ* is…

Choices:
- Dative with the compound verb: added to the law
- Accusative
- Genitive
- Nominative

Answer: Dative with the compound verb: added to the law

Why: *Προστίθημι*, “add to,” takes the dative of the thing added to.


@panel 112

*θαπτομένοις*

Question: *θαπτομένοις* is…

Choices:
- A present passive participle: those being buried
- An aorist active participle
- A finite verb
- An infinitive

Answer: A present passive participle: those being buried

Why: It agrees with *τοῖς* after *ἐπί*: over those who are buried.


@panel 113

*ἀγορεύεσθαι*

Question: *ἀγορεύεσθαι* is…

Choices:
- A passive infinitive: “to be spoken”
- A middle participle
- A future indicative
- An imperative

Answer: A passive infinitive: “to be spoken”

Why: Its subject is *αὐτόν*, the speech: that it be spoken.


@panel 114

**Xenophon, *Memorabilia* 1.1.1 (in the drill)**

πολλάκις ἐθαύμασα τίσι ποτὲ λόγοις Ἀθηναίους ἔπεισαν οἱ γραψάμενοι Σωκράτην ὡς ἄξιος εἴη θανάτου τῇ πόλει.

I have often wondered by what arguments those who indicted Socrates could have persuaded the Athenians that his life was justly forfeit to the state.
— H. G. Dakyns

**Context.** Xenophon begins his memoirs of Socrates by asking how the Athenians could have been persuaded to condemn him.


@panel 115

**The main clause.** *πολλάκις ἐθαύμασα*: *Ἐθαύμασα*, aorist, “I have wondered,” is the main verb.


@panel 116

**An indirect question.** *τίσι ποτὲ λόγοις Ἀθηναίους ἔπεισαν*: *Τίσι … λόγοις*, a dative of means, asks by what arguments; *ποτέ* strengthens the question.


@panel 117

**The subject.** *οἱ γραψάμενοι Σωκράτην*: *Οἱ γραψάμενοι*, the aorist middle participle with the article, means “those who indicted.”


@panel 118

**The optative of reported speech.** *ὡς ἄξιος εἴη θανάτου τῇ πόλει*: *Εἴη* is optative, standing after a past verb in reported speech: that he was worthy of death.


@panel 119

*τίσι*

Question: *τίσι … λόγοις* is…

Choices:
- A dative of means in an indirect question: by what arguments
- An indirect object
- A dative of possession
- A genitive

Answer: A dative of means in an indirect question: by what arguments

Why: The dative gives the means of persuading.


@panel 120

*οἱ γραψάμενοι*

Question: *οἱ γραψάμενοι* means…

Choices:
- “Those who indicted”: the middle of *γράφω* as a legal term
- “Those who wrote”
- “The writings”
- “They wrote”

Answer: “Those who indicted”: the middle of *γράφω* as a legal term

Why: In the middle voice, *γράφομαι* means to bring a written charge.


@panel 121

*εἴη*

Question: Why is *εἴη* optative?

Choices:
- It reports the charge after a past verb
- It expresses a wish
- It is a condition
- It is a purpose clause

Answer: It reports the charge after a past verb

Why: After a past tense, a reported statement may take the optative.


@panel 122

*θανάτου*

Question: Why is *θανάτου* genitive?

Choices:
- *ἄξιος*, “worthy,” takes the genitive
- It shows possession
- It follows *ὡς*
- It is a genitive absolute

Answer: *ἄξιος*, “worthy,” takes the genitive

Why: Adjectives of worth take the genitive of what one is worthy of.


@panel 123

**Plato, *Meno* 70a (in the drill)**

ἔχεις μοι εἰπεῖν, ὦ Σώκρατες, ἆρα διδακτὸν ἡ ἀρετή; ἢ οὐ διδακτὸν ἀλλʼ ἀσκητόν; ἢ οὔτε ἀσκητὸν οὔτε μαθητόν, ἀλλὰ φύσει παραγίγνεται τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἢ ἄλλῳ τινὶ τρόπῳ;

Can you tell me, Socrates, whether virtue is acquired by teaching or by practice; or if neither by teaching nor by practice, then whether it comes to man by nature, or in what other way?
— Benjamin Jowett

**Context.** The Meno opens without any preface: Meno asks Socrates whether virtue can be taught.


@panel 124

**Ἔχω with the infinitive.** *ἔχεις μοι εἰπεῖν, ὦ Σώκρατες*: *Ἔχεις εἰπεῖν*, “are you able to say,” uses *ἔχω* with the infinitive in the sense of “can.”


@panel 125

**A question with ἆρα.** *ἆρα διδακτὸν ἡ ἀρετή*: *Ἆρα* marks a question. *Διδακτόν*, neuter, is the predicate: is virtue a thing that can be taught?


@panel 126

**Alternatives.** *ἢ οὐ διδακτὸν ἀλλʼ ἀσκητόν*: *Ἤ* offers a second possibility, and *οὐ … ἀλλά* sets the two adjectives against each other.


@panel 127

**Datives of manner and of the person.** *ἀλλὰ φύσει παραγίγνεται τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἢ ἄλλῳ τινὶ τρόπῳ*: *Φύσει* and *ἄλλῳ τινὶ τρόπῳ* are datives of manner, and *τοῖς ἀνθρώποις* is the dative of the persons to whom it comes.


@panel 128

*ἔχεις μοι εἰπεῖν*

Question: *ἔχεις … εἰπεῖν* means…

Choices:
- “Can you say”: *ἔχω* with the infinitive
- “You have said”
- “Do you have a saying”
- “You will say”

Answer: “Can you say”: *ἔχω* with the infinitive

Why: *Ἔχω* with an infinitive means “be able.”


@panel 129

*ἆρα*

Question: *ἆρα* marks…

Choices:
- A question
- A wish
- A condition
- A command

Answer: A question

Why: *Ἆρα* introduces a question that expects no particular answer.


@panel 130

*διδακτὸν ἡ ἀρετή*

Question: Why is *διδακτόν* neuter, though *ἀρετή* is feminine?

Choices:
- A neuter predicate adjective means “a thing that is teachable”
- It agrees with an understood *ἔργον*
- It is a mistake
- *Ἀρετή* is neuter

Answer: A neuter predicate adjective means “a thing that is teachable”

Why: Greek may use a neuter predicate to speak of a thing in general.


@panel 131

*φύσει*

Question: *φύσει* is…

Choices:
- A dative of manner: by nature
- A verb
- A dative of the person
- A genitive

Answer: A dative of manner: by nature

Why: The dative gives the way in which virtue comes.


@panel 132

**Demosthenes, *First Philippic* 1 (in the drill)**

εἰ μὲν περὶ καινοῦ τινος πράγματος προυτίθετʼ, ὦ ἄνδρες Ἀθηναῖοι, λέγειν, ἐπισχὼν ἂν ἕως οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν εἰωθότων γνώμην ἀπεφήναντο, εἰ μὲν ἤρεσκέ τί μοι τῶν ὑπὸ τούτων ῥηθέντων, ἡσυχίαν ἂν ἦγον, εἰ δὲ μή, τότʼ ἂν καὐτὸς ἐπειρώμην ἃ γιγνώσκω λέγειν·

Had the question for debate been any thing new, Athenians, I should have waited till most of the usual speakers had been heard; if any of their counsels had been to my liking, I had remained silent, else proceeded to impart my own.
— Charles Rann Kennedy

**Context.** Demosthenes spoke his First Philippic in 351 BC, urging the Athenians to act against Philip of Macedon. He begins by explaining why he rises to speak first.


@panel 133

**A condition contrary to fact.** *εἰ μὲν περὶ καινοῦ τινος πράγματος προυτίθετʼ*: *Εἰ* with the imperfect *προυτίθετο* states a condition not true at present: if it were proposed to speak about a new matter.


@panel 134

**A participle with ἄν.** *ἐπισχὼν ἂν ἕως οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν εἰωθότων γνώμην ἀπεφήναντο*: *Ἐπισχὼν ἄν*, a participle with *ἄν*, carries the force of the conclusion: I would have waited until most of the usual speakers had declared their opinion.


@panel 135

**A second condition.** *εἰ μὲν ἤρεσκέ τί μοι τῶν ὑπὸ τούτων ῥηθέντων, ἡσυχίαν ἂν ἦγον*: *Εἰ* with the imperfect and *ἄν* with the imperfect: if anything they said pleased me, I would keep quiet.


@panel 136

**The contrary case.** *εἰ δὲ μή, τότʼ ἂν καὐτὸς ἐπειρώμην ἃ γιγνώσκω λέγειν*: *Εἰ δὲ μή*, “otherwise.” *Καὐτός* is *καὶ αὐτός* by crasis: I too would try to say what I think.


@panel 137

*προυτίθετʼ*

Question: *εἰ … προυτίθετο* is…

Choices:
- A condition contrary to fact, with the imperfect
- A simple condition
- A purpose clause
- A wish

Answer: A condition contrary to fact, with the imperfect

Why: The imperfect indicative with *εἰ*, and *ἄν* in the conclusion, mark a condition not true now.


@panel 138

*ἂν ἕως*

Question: What does *ἄν* with *ἐπισχών* do?

Choices:
- It gives the participle the force of the conclusion: “I would have waited”
- It marks a purpose
- It makes the participle future
- Nothing

Answer: It gives the participle the force of the conclusion: “I would have waited”

Why: A participle with *ἄν* stands for a finite verb with *ἄν*.


@panel 139

*ῥηθέντων*

Question: *ῥηθέντων* is…

Choices:
- An aorist passive participle: of the things said
- A perfect active participle
- A finite verb
- An infinitive

Answer: An aorist passive participle: of the things said

Why: *Ῥηθέντων* is the aorist passive participle of the verb “say,” genitive plural.


@panel 140

*καὐτὸς*

Question: *καὐτός* is…

Choices:
- *καὶ αὐτός* joined by crasis: “I too”
- A form of *κάω*
- A genitive
- An adverb of place

Answer: *καὶ αὐτός* joined by crasis: “I too”

Why: Crasis merges *καί* with the next word.


@panel 141

**The Gospel according to Luke, ** 2:1–3 (in the drill)**

Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις ἐξῆλθεν δόγμα παρὰ Καίσαρος Αὐγούστου ἀπογράφεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην· (αὕτη ἀπογραφὴ πρώτη ἐγένετο ἡγεμονεύοντος τῆς Συρίας Κυρηνίου·) καὶ ἐπορεύοντο πάντες ἀπογράφεσθαι, ἕκαστος εἰς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ πόλιν.

And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be taxed. (And this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria.) And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city.
— King James Version

**Context.** Luke begins his account of the birth of Jesus by placing it in the reign of Augustus.


@panel 142

**Ἐγένετο with a second verb.** *Ἐγένετο δὲ ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις ἐξῆλθεν δόγμα*: *Ἐγένετο*, “it came to pass,” is followed by a second finite verb, *ἐξῆλθεν*, a way of telling that follows the Hebrew style of the Greek Old Testament.


@panel 143

**An infinitive of the content.** *ἀπογράφεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην*: The infinitive gives the content of the decree: that the whole world be registered.


@panel 144

**A genitive absolute.** *ἡγεμονεύοντος τῆς Συρίας Κυρηνίου*: A participle and its noun in the genitive give the time: when Quirinius was governing Syria.


@panel 145

**An infinitive of purpose.** *καὶ ἐπορεύοντο πάντες ἀπογράφεσθαι*: *Ἀπογράφεσθαι* after a verb of going gives the purpose: they went to be registered.


@panel 146

*ἐξῆλθεν*

Question: *ἐξῆλθεν* is…

Choices:
- Aorist indicative, the second verb after *ἐγένετο*
- An infinitive
- A participle
- A subjunctive

Answer: Aorist indicative, the second verb after *ἐγένετο*

Why: Luke writes *ἐγένετο* and then a finite verb: it came to pass, a decree went out.


@panel 147

*ἀπογράφεσθαι πᾶσαν*

Question: *ἀπογράφεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην* gives…

Choices:
- The content of the decree, with the subject in the accusative
- The cause of the decree
- A purpose clause with ἵνα
- A genitive absolute

Answer: The content of the decree, with the subject in the accusative

Why: An infinitive with an accusative subject can state what is ordered.


@panel 148

*ἡγεμονεύοντος*

Question: *ἡγεμονεύοντος … Κυρηνίου* is…

Choices:
- A genitive absolute giving the time
- A genitive of possession
- The subject
- A dative

Answer: A genitive absolute giving the time

Why: The participle and its noun stand apart in the genitive.


@panel 149

*ἑαυτοῦ*

Question: *ἑαυτοῦ* is…

Choices:
- A reflexive pronoun: his own
- A personal pronoun “him”
- A relative pronoun
- A demonstrative

Answer: A reflexive pronoun: his own

Why: The reflexive refers back to the subject, *ἕκαστος*.
